newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore refiners back in profit, but woes remain.
newsitem.headline: Singapore refiners back in profit, but woes remain.

text.p: Battered Singapore refiners are enjoying profits for the first time in 1997, but are unlikely to reverse production cuts soon as prices of some oil products remain too weak, industry sources said on Wednesday.

"The view we have taken is that the profits are temporary... we need crude oil (prices) to go down or gas oil to go up further. No action will be taken to raise production immediately," a source at a major refiner said.

Singapore refining margins returned to the black this week following a $1.20 per barrel drop in benchmark North Sea Brent March crude futures on the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX) over the Lunar New Year holidays.
Refiners are now enjoying profits of about 40 cents per barrels on the first stage of processing compared to losses of more than $1.00 per barrel in January.
Refiners rely on being able to sell products at prices high enough to cover the cost of buying and processing crude oil and provide a return on their massive investments.
Sources said oil companies might restore production to full capacity in March when two refiners, Singapore Refining Co (SRC) and Mobil Singapore are scheduled to carry out major maintenance programs.
Currently, two refiners in Singapore are operating below maximum capacity.

Shell Singapore cut output on January 17 by about seven percent at its 435,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) refinery while Esso Singapore reduced runs by 20 to 25 percent at its 230,000 bpd refinery at the same time.

SRC said it plans to shut down a 90,000 bpd crude distillation unit (CDU) for 22 days at its 285,000 bpd refinery and Mobil is expected to shutdown its 280,000 bpd refinery from mid-March for six weeks, sources said.
SRC is co-owned by Singapore Petroleum Corp, British Petroleum and Caltex, a joint-venture of U.S. majors Chevron Corp and Texaco Inc.
As a result, Singapore will lose about 25 percent of its 1.2 million bpd refining capacity.
The reduction in output may not necessarily lead to higher prices as there are enough supplies in the region to meet current low demands, traders said.
"The market will only pick up if China returns to buy in a big way as it did last December," one trader said.
China bought a record one million tonnes of diesel and 600,000-tonnes of fuel oil in December but more than halved its purchases in Janaury due to skyrocketting prices.
Following China's decision to cut purchases, prices of both products collapsed, precipitating the losses at refineries.

Diesel prices fell from a near six-year peak of $34.45 per barrel in early December to trade on Tuesday at $25.10 per barrel while fuel oil traded last week at $93.00 per tonne--$31 per tonne below its end December peak.
